evidence: change-product-status.dto.ts: ChangeProductStatusDto.status is declared with @IsIn(['ACTIVE', 'INACTIVE', 'DELETED']), and its comment calls this 'a deliberate duplication of a closed set' from ProductStatus.

change-product-status.command-handler.ts: execute() validates the same set again with ProductStatus.fromNameIgnoreCase<ProductStatus>(status), and builds the accepted-values message from ProductStatus.getAll<ProductStatus>().map((candidate) => candidate.name).
The copies already disagree: @IsIn is case-sensitive, while fromNameIgnoreCase ignores case, so each enforces a different rule.
change-product-status.command.ts: the ChangeProductStatusCommand constructor takes a ChangeProductStatusDto and copies dto.status, which ties the command to the transport DTO.
change-product-status.service.ts: ChangeProductStatusService.execute builds the command and sends it on the CommandBus, which uses the module's command abstraction consistently.
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
The four files cover one concern: the change-product-status use case. The service builds ChangeProductStatusCommand and sends it on the CommandBus. ChangeProductStatusCommandHandler loads the product, changes its status, checks broken rules, saves and commits.

However, the set of valid statuses is defined twice within the unit. ChangeProductStatusDto hard-codes @IsIn(['ACTIVE', 'INACTIVE', 'DELETED']). The handler validates the same set again through ProductStatus.fromNameIgnoreCase and ProductStatus.getAll().

The two copies have already drifted: @IsIn is case-sensitive, while the handler ignores case. A value like 'inactive' is rejected by the DTO but would be accepted by the handler.

The DTO comment says the copy is deliberate, so that a bad status returns a 400 naming the accepted values. That reason doesn't require a literal copy: the DTO could take its list from ProductStatus.getAll().map(s => s.name) and keep a single source of truth. The handler already turns an unknown name into an InvalidFormatException naming the accepted values.

Minor point: ChangeProductStatusCommand's constructor takes the transport DTO instead of plain values, which ties the command to the HTTP contract. The concrete ProductRepository injection is an import-direction question and is out of scope.

violations.message: ChangeProductStatusDto hard-codes @IsIn(['ACTIVE', 'INACTIVE', 'DELETED']), copying the closed set that ProductStatus already defines and that the command handler checks again with ProductStatus.fromNameIgnoreCase. The copies have drifted: the DTO is case-sensitive, the handler is not. Take the allowed values from ProductStatus.getAll() so the set is defined in one place.
